question: Despite the government’s claims that electricity prices would fall, figures published by Greece's Independent Power Transmission Operator (ADMIE) show that in 2023 electricity prices went up by 85% compared to 2019 when the SYRIZA government introduced the energy exchange initiative. The weighted average has increased by 133.3% compared to 2015.

The five biggest power companies that have a monopoly over the Greek electricity market made a total profit before tax of EUR 1.6 billion, up by more than 50% compared to 2021. This trend will continue in 2023. With this in mind: 1.

What view does the Commission take of the fact that, despite the announcements and promises regarding a reduction in pricing and guaranteed low electricity prices, in the end, the EU's energy liberalisation strategy, the green ‘transition’ and the energy exchange initiative, are placing the burden on workers so that energy companies can secure a profit?

What view does it take of the fact that tailoring the energy mix to suit the needs and interests of business groups, with natural gas being used as a ‘transitional fuel’, phasing out dependency on Russian gas only to replace it with more expensive American LNG that is harmful to the environment, and the measures to boost the renewable energy share based on the terms of the ‘liberalised market’, entrench and raise the high prices working families have to pay, to double or more what they paid three years ago?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.3.2024) The Commission follows with interest the recently introduced colour-coded electricity pricing scheme in Greece. Regarding the specific questions, the Commission recalls the following.

To fortify resilience against high, volatile prices and draw on lessons from the energy crisis1, the Commission introduced its electricity market reform proposal2, that has been provisionally agreed by the co-legislators3. This reform will make the market future-proof to maximise the benefits of affordable clean energy, better protect EU consumers from price spikes and empower them in the green energy transition.

It aims to reduce supplier failure risks, to strengthen consumer protection, offer consumers varied contract options and clearer information. EU Member States determine their energy mix, while adhering to Treaty and in particular internal market rules and factoring in common climate goals.

The primary objective of a wellfunctioning market is to foster a secure supply of energy, while always relying on the cheapest and cleanest sources available. The EU has been working with trusted global partners to diversify supplies, securing higher deliveries of pipeline gas and record liquefied natural gas imports.

This work, combined with collective efforts to reduce EU gas demand and to ensure adequate filling of storage facilities, has allowed the EU to considerably strengthen the security of its energy supply. In this policy context, reducing the methane emissions along the natural gas value chain is a priority of the EU’s energy and climate objectives.
